wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for apple butter: apples cooked in apple cider and vinegar, pressed into a pulp, cooked with white and brown sugar and spices, and processed in a boiling-water bath.

akapity: NCHFP uses 8 pounds (about 3.6 kg) of apples, 2 cups of apple cider, 2 cups of vinegar, 2 1/4 cups of white sugar, 2 1/4 cups of packed brown sugar, 2 tablespoons of ground cinnamon and 1 tablespoon of ground cloves; this makes about 9 to 10 pint jars.
Despite the name, apple butter contains no butter: it is a thick, spiced apple pulp cooked with sugar.
NCHFP suggests Jonathan, Winesap, Stayman, Golden Delicious, McIntosh or other tasty apple varieties.
Use fresh apples, free from any signs of decay or mold.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
The recipe does not give the strength of the vinegar; JarAtlas rule (cautious): use white distilled or cider vinegar labelled 5% or 6% acidity, and do not dilute 10% vinegar with water to make 5%.
Sterilize the half-pint and pint jars; NCHFP says quart jars need not be presterilized.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Wash the apples, remove the stems, cut them into quarters and remove the cores.
Cook them slowly in the apple cider and vinegar until soft.
Press the fruit through a colander, food mill or strainer.
Cook the pulp with the sugar and spices, stirring frequently.
To test for doneness, take a spoonful and hold it away from the steam for 2 minutes: the butter is done if it stays mounded on the spoon.
Another test: spoon a little onto a plate; when no rim of liquid separates around the edge, the butter is ready for canning.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
Fill the hot apple butter into the jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Put on the lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes and quart jars for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process half-pints and pints for 10 minutes and quarts for 15 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process half-pints and pints for 15 minutes and quarts for 20 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so JarAtlas recommends smaller jars.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): a jar of up to 473 ml gets the shorter pint time, so sterilize it like a pint jar.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): this card gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): keep an opened jar in the refrigerator; NCHFP says this for its reduced-sugar apple butter and for opened jams and jellies, but gives no storage time for this apple butter after opening.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
If you see mold or other signs of spoilage in an opened jar, throw out its whole contents.
